screens.title: Download Fabric Binaries and Docker Images
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll learn why and how to download the actual Hyperledger Fabric executables and Docker images. The repository you cloned contains configurations and helper scripts, but not the runtime binaries or images themselves. The bootstrap. sh script automates two essential steps: it fetches and extracts the Fabric CLI binaries and then pulls the pre-built Docker images for peers, orderers, the certificate authority, and optional state databases. We'll show the canonical command used for an example release, explain the key arguments, and demonstrate how to verify the results. You'll also learn common causes of failure such as missing execute permissions or network interruptions, and how to resolve them quickly. By the end of this overview you will understand why matching the Fabric versions to your release branch matters, how the script places binaries in the bin directory and how to confirm that the images are present locally. Think about when a missing binary or image could stop your network from starting, and how this step prevents that problem.

screens.title: What bootstrap.sh does
screens.narratorSegment: The bootstrap. sh script is a purpose-built helper inside the fabric-samples repository that automates fetching the two categories of artifacts you need to run Fabric: command-line binaries and Docker images. Conceptually, the repository contains sample configurations and helper scripts, not the runtime code. The script first uses curl to download a compressed tarball of binaries and extracts them into the fabric-samples/bin directory. These binaries include the peer and orderer CLIs, configtxgen and cryptogen for creating channel artifacts and cryptographic material, and the fabric-ca-client for interacting with a Certificate Authority. Second, bootstrap. sh runs docker pull for a curated list of image names and tags that match the Fabric release you requested. These images include peer, orderer, ca, and tools, and optionally state databases such as couchdb when your docker-compose files reference them. A common misconception is that cloning fabric-samples gives you everything you need; it does not. The bootstrap step bridges that gap. Example: when you cloned release-2.5, use the matching 2.5.0 binaries and images so the configuration files and binaries are compatible. That version match reduces runtime errors when you start containers and execute Fabric CLI commands.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: bootstrap.sh automates downloading Fabric command-line tools and pulling the Docker images required to run a Fabric network.

content.html:
Core Concept
What bootstrap.sh does
A precise definition and practical implications.
• Downloads a binaries tarball via curl and extracts to bin/ so CLI tools are available.
• Pulls recommended Docker images using docker pull so containers for peers and orderers are ready.
• Ensures the fetched versions match the fabric-samples release to avoid compatibility issues.
• Does not clone sample configs when run with the -s flag; that flag skips cloning because you already have the repository.
Key Takeaway

bootstrap.sh is the bridge from sample config to runnable Fabric components; run it early in setup.

Analogy
Think of fabric-samples as a car's manual and bootstrap.sh as the parts delivery that brings the engine and wheels. The manual alone isn’t enough to move the car.
Concrete example
cd ~/fabric-dev/fabric-samples
# Execute the bootstrap script for Fabric version 2.5.0
./scripts/bootstrap.sh 2.5.0 1.5.0 -s
This example downloads binaries for 2.5.0 and CA 1.5.0 and skips re-cloning samples.

screens.title: Two primary actions of the script
screens.narratorSegment: When you run bootstrap. sh it follows a predictable two-step process: download and extract the CLI binaries, then pull the Docker images. Step one uses curl to fetch a tarball hosted for the requested Fabric release. The script extracts the tarball into fabric-samples/bin so the tools like peer, orderer, configtxgen, cryptogen and fabric-ca-client are available in that directory. These tools are used for channel creation, certificate generation, and administrative operations. Step two runs docker pull commands for a curated list of images that match the same release tag: hyperledger/fabric-peer, hyperledger/fabric-orderer, hyperledger/fabric-ca, hyperledger/fabric-tools, and optional images such as hyperledger/fabric-couchdb if referenced by your compose files. Pulling images prepares the runtime artifacts so containers can be created later. A common misconception is that the images are small; some are large and pulling them can take significant time depending on your connection. That’s why the script shows verbose output and why the -s flag exists to avoid re-cloning when unnecessary. This two-step flow simplifies reproducible local setup for your Fabric network. Two primary actions of the script means bootstrap.sh first downloads/extracts binaries, then pulls docker images; both are required for a runnable fabric environment.. In practical terms, stepwise breakdown: binaries then docker images. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Process Flow
Two primary actions of bootstrap.sh
1
Download and extract binaries

Pull Docker images

Command anatomy

Change into your fabric-samples directory and run the script with the Fabric and CA versions that match your cloned branch. content.html:
Terminal Demo
cd ~/fabric-dev/fabric-samples
# Execute the bootstrap script for Fabric version 2.5.0 and CA 1.5.0
./scripts/bootstrap.sh 2.5.0 1.5.0 -s

# After script completes, verify images and binaries
docker images | grep hyperledger
ls bin/
./bin/peer version
This sequence runs the fetch, then checks that images are present and the peer binary responds. Expect verbose output during downloads; be patient on slower connections.
Watch points & quick fixes
  • Permission denied: run chmod +x scripts/bootstrap.sh and retry.
  • curl or docker pull failures: check internet connectivity and firewall settings.
  • Commands not found after script: export PATH=$PATH:$(pwd)/bin for current session or call ./bin/.
Pro tip: use -s when you already have the repository to avoid duplicate cloning steps.

screens.title: Binaries vs Docker images
screens.narratorSegment: It's important to understand the difference between the binaries bootstrap. sh installs and the Docker images it pulls. Binaries are standalone executable tools placed in the bin directory. They are used directly from your host: you run the peer CLI to interact with peers, run configtxgen to create channel configuration transactions, and cryptogen to generate keys when needed. These tools are useful in administrative scripts and CI tasks that run on your workstation. Docker images, by contrast, are packaged runtime environments used to create containers that host peers, orderers, CAs, and optional databases. When you start your network with docker-compose, those images become running containers. A common misconception is that binaries are sufficient to run the network; they are not. Binaries let you manage and interact with the network, but the network nodes themselves run inside the Docker containers created from the images. Both are necessary: images provide the environment, binaries provide control and artifact generation outside or inside containers. Keeping the versions aligned avoids subtle runtime mismatches. Binaries vs Docker images means binaries are cli tools for administration; docker images are runtime environments for the network nodes—both are required.. In practical terms, understand the different roles each artifact plays. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Binaries are CLI tools for administration; Docker images are runtime environments for the network nodes—both are required.

content.html:
Comparison
Binaries
• Extracted to fabric-samples/bin • Run on the host or in a tools container • Examples: peer, orderer, configtxgen, cryptogen, fabric-ca-client
Use binaries to generate artifacts, inspect versions, and run management commands.
Comparison
Docker images
• Pulled into local Docker image store • Used to run containers for peers, orderers, CA, tools, and optional DBs • Examples: hyperledger/fabric-peer, fabric-orderer, fabric-ca, fabric-tools, fabric-couchdb
Images are the runtime; containers created from them host the network components.
Common mistake

Assuming binaries alone let you run peers. You still need images to create the node containers.

screens.title: Key binaries you will get
screens.narratorSegment: The bootstrap script installs several critical executables into the bin directory. The peer binary is the primary command-line interface used to interact with peer nodes: installing and invoking chaincode, joining channels, and querying ledgers. The orderer binary provides administrative interfaces for orderer nodes and can be used when you run orderer processes locally. Configtxgen generates channel configuration transactions and anchor peer updates; it translates configuration templates into artifacts that the orderer and channels consume. Cryptogen is a simple tool to generate cryptographic material—certificates and keys—for organizations and nodes when you are not using a CA. Finally, fabric-ca-client is the client that interacts with a Fabric Certificate Authority, used when you decide to generate certificates via a CA rather than cryptogen. Each tool has a narrow but crucial role: together they let you prepare and manage the network's configuration and security artifacts. If any of these are missing or version-mismatched, commands may fail or produce incompatible artifacts. Key binaries you will get means peer, orderer, configtxgen, cryptogen and fabric-ca-client each perform specific setup and admin duties for your fabric network.. In practical terms, what each tool is used for in network setup. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. keyIdea.text: peer, orderer, configtxgen, cryptogen and fabric-ca-client each perform specific setup and admin duties for your Fabric network.

content.html:
peer
CLI for interacting with peer nodes: install and invoke chaincode, join channels, and query ledgers.
orderer
CLI and binary for control and administrative actions related to ordering service nodes.
configtxgen
Generates channel creation transactions and configuration artifacts for the ordering system.
cryptogen
Simple utility to generate certificates and keys for organizations and peers when not using a CA.
fabric-ca-client
Client tool to enroll and register identities with a Fabric CA; used when certificate authority-based flows are chosen.
Key Takeaway

Each binary plays a specific role in generating artifacts, administering components, or interacting with the CA; missing any can block setup.

screens.title: Core Docker images pulled
screens.narratorSegment: Bootstrap will pull a set of Hyperledger Fabric images required to run the network. The primary images include hyperledger/fabric-peer for peer nodes, hyperledger/fabric-orderer for ordering service nodes, hyperledger/fabric-ca for the Certificate Authority, and hyperledger/fabric-tools, a utility image often used for administrative tasks within a containerized environment. Optionally, if your docker-compose files reference a state database, the script can pull hyperledger/fabric-couchdb. Historically some deployments used Kafka-related images for ordering; if your compose specifies Kafka-based ordering you might pull those images as well. Each image corresponds to a runnable service: pulling them ensures docker-compose can start containers without needing to download at runtime. When an image pull fails, docker images will not list it locally. Verifying with docker images | grep hyperledger gives a quick view of what is present. Note that image tags must align with your Fabric version to maintain compatibility between the runtime and the CLI tools you installed earlier. Core Docker images
  • hyperledger/fabric-peer — runtime for peer nodes
  • hyperledger/fabric-orderer — runtime for orderer nodes
  • hyperledger/fabric-ca — Certificate Authority runtime
  • hyperledger/fabric-tools — utility image for admin/debugging tasks

In this lesson you'll learn why and how to download the actual Hyperledger Fabric executables and Docker images. The repository you cloned contains configurations and helper scripts, but not the runtime binaries or images themselves. The bootstrap. sh script automates two essential steps: it fetches and extracts the Fabric CLI binaries and then pulls the pre-built Docker images for peers, orderers, the certificate authority, and optional state databases. We'll show the canonical command used for an example release, explain the key arguments, and demonstrate how to verify the results. You'll also learn common causes of failure such as missing execute permissions or network interruptions, and how to resolve them quickly. By the end of this overview you will understand why matching the Fabric versions to your release branch matters, how the script places binaries in the bin directory and how to confirm that the images are present locally. Think about when a missing binary or image could stop your network from starting, and how this step prevents that problem.

By the end of this chapter you will execute the bootstrap script, identify the binaries it installs, list the Docker images it pulls, and confidently troubleshoot common failures. First, you will run the script inside a cloned fabric-samples repository so the correct versions are fetched. Second, you will recognize the essential command-line utilities — for example the peer tool, orderer tool, configtxgen and cryptogen — and know their roles in network configuration and cryptographic material generation. Third, you will list and explain the core Docker images like fabric-peer, fabric-orderer, fabric-ca and fabric-tools, and understand optional images such as couchdb when used as a state database. Finally, you will diagnose and resolve typical problems: network interruptions causing curl or docker pull to fail, and permission errors that prevent script execution. Each objective includes a brief practical check: run a command or inspect a directory. These capabilities keep your local setup reliable and let you move from sample configs to a running Fabric network quickly.

This continuation focuses on verification and hands-on checks you should perform after running the script. You will list local Docker images to confirm that hyperledger images are present, and list the bin directory to ensure the binaries were extracted. You will run simple commands such as the peer version check to confirm the executable works. These verification steps reduce guesswork: they show whether downloads completed successfully and whether your environment can run Fabric commands. You will also practice two quick fixes: adding the bin directory to your PATH for the session or invoking the executable with a relative path. Finally, you will learn to capture the outputs that prove success—these are the same items you would screenshot in a lab. These verification skills are small but essential; without them you may try to start a network that lacks the required runtime components.

The bootstrap. sh script is a purpose-built helper inside the fabric-samples repository that automates fetching the two categories of artifacts you need to run Fabric: command-line binaries and Docker images. Conceptually, the repository contains sample configurations and helper scripts, not the runtime code. The script first uses curl to download a compressed tarball of binaries and extracts them into the fabric-samples/bin directory. These binaries include the peer and orderer CLIs, configtxgen and cryptogen for creating channel artifacts and cryptographic material, and the fabric-ca-client for interacting with a Certificate Authority. Second, bootstrap. sh runs docker pull for a curated list of image names and tags that match the Fabric release you requested. These images include peer, orderer, ca, and tools, and optionally state databases such as couchdb when your docker-compose files reference them. A common misconception is that cloning fabric-samples gives you everything you need; it does not. The bootstrap step bridges that gap. Example: when you cloned release-2.5, use the matching 2.5.0 binaries and images so the configuration files and binaries are compatible. That version match reduces runtime errors when you start containers and execute Fabric CLI commands.

When you run bootstrap. sh it follows a predictable two-step process: download and extract the CLI binaries, then pull the Docker images. Step one uses curl to fetch a tarball hosted for the requested Fabric release. The script extracts the tarball into fabric-samples/bin so the tools like peer, orderer, configtxgen, cryptogen and fabric-ca-client are available in that directory. These tools are used for channel creation, certificate generation, and administrative operations. Step two runs docker pull commands for a curated list of images that match the same release tag: hyperledger/fabric-peer, hyperledger/fabric-orderer, hyperledger/fabric-ca, hyperledger/fabric-tools, and optional images such as hyperledger/fabric-couchdb if referenced by your compose files. Pulling images prepares the runtime artifacts so containers can be created later. A common misconception is that the images are small; some are large and pulling them can take significant time depending on your connection. That’s why the script shows verbose output and why the -s flag exists to avoid re-cloning when unnecessary. This two-step flow simplifies reproducible local setup for your Fabric network. Remember three core ideas from this chapter. First, fabric-samples contains sample configuration and scripts but not the runtime artifacts; bootstrap. sh fills that gap by downloading binaries and pulling images. Second, the binaries such as peer, orderer, configtxgen and cryptogen are host tools for generating artifacts and managing network operations, while Docker images are runtime environments for nodes; both are required for a functioning network. Third, verification and troubleshooting are straightforward: list Docker images to confirm pulls, check the bin directory and run peer version, grant execute permissions if the script cannot run, and ensure your network connection and Docker daemon are operational. These three points—fetch, verify, and troubleshoot—cover the routine tasks that prevent setup failures. Keep these concepts in mind as you prepare the environment for subsequent hands-on network creation and testing.
